input.question: If someone receives a full organ transplant will the organ be eventually replaced by the host's cells or will it remain as the the donor's cells for the rest of the host's life.
input.ground_truth: It will always be the donor's cells. It can be possible to wean off of antirejection drugs as your body gets used to the new organ, but if your whole liver is replaced by a donor liver, you do not have any of your own liver cells to replicate and replace the donor cells.

Okay, let’s imagine the person’s body is like a big garden, and the new organ (like a heart or kidney) is like a special plant you put in the garden from someone else.

When you put that new plant in the garden, most of the time, the soil and the garden around it are from your own garden. But the plant itself—the new organ—starts with the donor’s cells, which are like the plant’s seeds and roots.

Now, sometimes, a few of your garden’s own cells might sneak in and help the new plant grow a little, but most of the plant stays the same as when it came from the donor. So, for many years, the organ is mostly made of the donor’s cells. But over a very long time, some of your body’s cells might slowly replace a tiny bit of the donor’s cells, but not all of them.

So, the new organ is mostly the donor’s cells for a long, long time, but not forever—because your body is always trying to fix and change things a little bit.
